questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Asymptotes of a Vertical Hyperbola by Completing the Square
questions.problem: Calculate the asymptotes of the hyperbola $16{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+4x+64y+44=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to group the $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}+4x+64y+44 & =0 \\ 16{y}^{2}+64y-{x}^{2}+4x & =-44 \\ 16[{y}^{2}+4y]-[{x}^{2}-4x] & =-44 \\ 16[(y+2)^{2}-4]-[(x-2)^{2}-4] & =-44 \\ 16(y+2)^{2}-64-(x-2)^{2}+4 & =-44 \\ 16(y+2)^{2}-(x-2)^{2} & =-44+64-4 \\ 16(y+2)^{2}-(x-2)^{2} & =16 \\ \frac{16(y+2)^{2}}{16}-\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{16} & =\frac{16}{16} \\ (y+2)^{2}-\frac{(x-2)^{2}}{16} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The asymptotes of a vertical hyperbola

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
y-k=\pm \frac{a}{b}(x-h).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
(h,k)=(2,-2),\,a=\sqrt{1}=1,\,b=\sqrt{16}=4.
$$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are

$$
\begin{aligned}y+2 & =\pm \frac{1}{4}(x-2).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Calculate the asymptotes of the hyperbola 
${y}^{2}-25{x}^{2}-4y+50x-46=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
To rewrite the equation of the hyperbola in standard form, we need to group the $x$ and $y$ terms and complete the squares, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-25{x}^{2}-4y+50x-46 & =0 \\ {y}^{2}-4y-25{x}^{2}+50x-46 & =0 \\ [{y}^{2}-4y]-25[{x}^{2}-2x]-46 & =0 \\ [(y-2)^{2}-4]-25[(x-1)^{2}-1]-46 & =0 \\ (y-2)^{2}-4-25(x-1)^{2}+25-46 & =0 \\ (y-2)^{2}-25(x-1)^{2} & =46+4-25 \\ (y-2)^{2}-25(x-1)^{2} & =25 \\ \frac{(y-2)^{2}}{25}-(x-1)^{2} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

The asymptotes of a vertical hyperbola

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1
$$

are given by 

$$
y-k=\pm \frac{a}{b}(x-h).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
(h,k)=(1,2),\,a=\sqrt{25}=5,\,b=\sqrt{1}=1.
$$

Therefore, the asymptotes of the hyperbola are

$$
y-2=\pm 5(x-1).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Asymptotes of a Vertical Hyperbola Given in Standard Form
questions.worked_solution:
The standard equation of a vertical hyperbola centered at $(h,k)$ is

$$
\frac{(y-k)^{2}}{{a}^{2}}-\frac{(x-h)^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

For a vertical hyperbola, the equations of the asymptotes are

$$
y-k=\pm \frac{a}{b}(x-h).
$$

In our case, we have 

$$
(h,k)=(-3,0),\,a=\sqrt{12}=2\sqrt{3},\,b=\sqrt{27}=3\sqrt{3}.
$$

 

Therefore, the asymptotes are given by

$$
\begin{aligned}y-0 & =\pm (\frac{2\sqrt{3}}{3\sqrt{3}})(x-(-3)) \\ y & =\pm \,\frac{2}{3}(x+3).\end{aligned}
$$

$$

In our case, we have 

$$
(h,k)=(0,-4),\,a=\sqrt{8}=2\sqrt{2},\,b=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt{2}.
